publisher: State University of New York Press
essay_title: Heidegger as Rhetor: Hans-Georg Gadamer Interviewed by Ansgar Kemmann

author.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
author.affiliation_at_time: emeritus, University of Heidelberg (Karl Jaspers chair)

essay_thesis_one_sentence: Aristotle's *Rhetoric* I.2 defines rhetoric correctly as *dynamis* (a power belonging to being-human), not as a *technē* — and Heidegger's 1924 lecture course made this *dynamis*-of-*logos*-grounded-in-*pathē* into the hermeneutics of facticity that survives in *Truth and Method*; what Heidegger lost was not the rhetorical insight but the conversational form proper to it.

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: I. BIOGRAPHICAL INTRODUCTION
argumentative_actions: Gadamer recounts his 1923 arrival in Freiburg as 'messenger from Marburg' (sent by Natorp and Hartmann) and his being 'completely enthralled' by Heidegger's 1922 'Natorp Report' (n. 1).

Reports the *invitation* to read Aristotle privately with Heidegger — 'one alone once a week in the evening' — and the *grasping*, 'to my great surprise, that *logos* has something to do with speaking. In Marburg's Neo-Kantianism logos was just "reason."' (book p. 47)
Cites the SS 1923 *phronēsis* seminar in Freiburg as 'igniting my thinking to a much greater degree' (book p. 48).

Establishes himself as a *classical philologist by training* — under Lommatzsch (n. 3) and Friedländer (n. 4) — studying Cicero, Quintilian, Attic and Roman rhetoric, Plato's *Symposium*. Gadamer locates 'the origin of my hermeneutics' in Plato's 'You will not understand what I will now say' (book p. 48).

Concedes a key absence: 'the topic that chiefly interested Heidegger at that time, the *pathē* doctrine, this aspect of Aristotle's rhetoric — that you correctly remark Heidegger especially emphasized then — that topic I did not understand at the time. I was still too immature for that.' (book p. 48) — this confession frames the entire interview as a retrospective reckoning with what the young Gadamer missed.

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: II. ON THE STATUS OF RHETORIC
argumentative_actions: Kemmann's question (italicized) frames the issue: Gadamer in two recent conversations (Kühne-Bertram & Rodi 1997-98; Grondin 1997) had defended 'the very broad concept of rhetoric' that 'contained all the humanities until modern times' (n. 5, n. 6).
Gadamer pivots to Heidegger as the source of his own narrower rhetoric-as-rhetoric reading: Heidegger 'referred directly to Aristotle and already established rhetoric as the *dynamis* of humans.'

Quotes Heidegger directly (n. 7 = GA 18, 114): 'Aristotle defined rhetoric (1.2) as *dynamis*. This definition is to be retained even though Aristotle often designates it as *technē*. This designation is incorrect, whereas *dynamis* is the correct definition.' This is the volume's locus classicus on tension VT2.
Kemmann presses: 'What is at stake in this alternative (technē/dynamis)?' — the analytical question that organizes the rest of the interview.

Gadamer responds: *technē* is 'a very general expression, *if* one did not mean mathematics specifically' — Heidegger 'was still using *technē*, until he began emphatically using the concept of *energeia*. And so he associated the concept of *dynamis* with the concept of *energeia*, and missed the other one' [INTERP-low: Gadamer's 'missed the other one' refers to the *technē*-side associations that Heidegger did *not* preserve in his eventual *dynamis–energeia* coupling — i.e., the productive/poietic dimension that *technē* would have grafted onto *dynamis*].

Concludes (book p. 49): 'Even from today's perspective, I would want, like Heidegger, to characterize rhetoric as more a *dynamis*. That should indicate that rhetoric belongs to being human and is not just an occasional ability. Actually, everyone is a speaker.'
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_structure: doctrinal apologia with one citation as fulcrum

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: III. THE RHETORIC OF PHILOSOPHY: USING THE EXAMPLE OF MARTIN HEIDEGGER
argumentative_actions: Kemmann opens with a Heidegger quotation from SS 1924 (n. 8 = GA 18, 169f): 'I only wish to point out that it might be more appropriate if philosophers could decide to consider what speaking to others really means.' Gadamer reads this as Heidegger's general critique of philosophers who 'lose sight of speaking to someone.'

Targets named: 'Richard Kroner in Freiburg and Nicolai Hartmann in Marburg', plus Husserl ('he actually never tried to hide his admiration for Husserl, at least not at that time'). Hartmann is contrasted with Heidegger as a teacher: Hartmann was 'a knight — so aristocratic and reserved' but successful teaching 'was clearly on Heidegger's side.'

Heidegger's lectures: 'enormously fascinating — oh yes, rhetorically masterful! ... had an enormous radiance.' 'That Aristotle suddenly became a phenomenologist was exactly what Heidegger accomplished and was quite the exception.'

Personal disclosure on the *anti-conversational* Heidegger: 'It was very difficult to speak with Heidegger because he wanted to understand step by step. So he did not terribly much like to discuss with me. I understood too quickly. He didn't like that; he needed the steps.' (book p. 50) — Gadamer's hermeneutics emerges *in contrast* to this: Gadamer privileges *Gespräch* (conversation, discussing [Reden]) over Heidegger's *Vortrag* (lecture).
Anecdote — Hannah Arendt: 'How he educated Hannah Arendt!' 'an interesting, talented Jewess' — Gadamer reports the secrecy of the affair, his own ignorance, the friend Jakob Klein's misjudgment.

On Heidegger's audience-relation: 'It was not an exchange with the audience. He tried too hard to find himself' (book p. 51). 'Naturally it was not an exchange with the audience' as a contrast to the Bultmann-Heidegger collaboration which 'worked completely.'

On rhetorical *mastery* vs. *substance*: 'those who conduct their lectures using too much of their rhetorical ability are not the best teachers' (Eugen Kühnemann, Breslau 'ghastly' — n. 14). 'To that extent Heidegger was much more substantive.'

Anti-Latin pivot (book p. 52): 'behind all of Heidegger, there was the wish to overcome the Latin elements in the language of philosophy ... "*Diskussion*" — I can say what I want, but it is, of course, just Latin.' Heidegger 'always strove to find the natural German language.'

Scheler death anecdote (n. 9, May 1928 obituary printed in *Metaphysische Anfangsgründe der Logik* GA 26): Gadamer's reporting of Heidegger's reactive 'malice' against Scheler, then the *de partibus animae* / *animal*-correction story (book pp. 52-53) — Heidegger had publicly accused Scheler of citing a non-existent Aristotelian text; Gadamer privately supplied the philological correction (anima → animal), and Heidegger publicly retracted. Gadamer reads this as Heidegger 'become possessed by something but also immensely accomplished in extracting himself.'

Quotes Heidegger on the SS 1924 lecture's aim (n. 11 = *Ontologie. Hermeneutik der Faktizität* = GA 63 cited via n. 10 'GA 18, 3' for the next quote; n. 12 = GA 63, 329): 'The lecture does not aim at something philosophical. It concerns the understanding of basic concepts in their conceptuality. The aim is philological and is to practice somewhat more the reading of philosophers' [GA 18, 3 per n. 10]. Concluding (n. 12 from same volume, 329): 'What is at stake is not to say something new, but to say what the Ancients really meant.' Kemmann presses: 'Does this remark indicate a genuine philosophical point — or does it concern "mere rhetoric"?'

Gadamer's response: the closing sentence is 'his colossal demand' — what is at stake is *to say only what the Ancients meant*. The opening 'self-defense' (saying-the-lecture-is-not-philosophical) is to deflect 'the warranted suspicion that he just wanted to push his own views.' Underneath the apologetic frame is a genuine philosophical thesis (book p. 53).

On Heidegger's view of teaching (n. 13 = GA 63, 327): 'to speak to another, approach the other in the manner of communicating. The actual being of a teacher is: to stand before an other and to speak to him, and in such a way that the other, listening, follows him.' Gadamer's reaction: 'Listening follows him!' (book p. 53) — this exclamation is the section's affective climax.

Closing: Gadamer's own discovery, through teaching philosophy at Leipzig (n. 15 = 1938-1947), that 'the conversation with the audience is sometimes present even in written texts. Actually all of my works were spoken' (book p. 55) — establishing the *Gespräch*-character of his entire corpus.
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_structure: interlocking biographical-philosophical anecdotes building toward 'Listening follows him!' climax; Q&A turns are dense with single-anecdote → philosophical-extraction pattern

section_2_hierarchical_outline.heading: IV. THE PHILOSOPHY OF RHETORIC IN THE UNIVERSE OF LINGUISTICALITY [SPRACHLICHKEIT]
argumentative_actions: Kemmann opens (book p. 55) with the SS 1924 thesis (n. 16 = GA 18, 117): rhetoric 'concerns speaking as a basic mode of human being, as being with one another'; understanding *legein* presents 'new aspects concerning the comprehension of the being of being with one another.'

Kemmann notes the *later* Heidegger 'distanced himself from a nominalistic philosophy of language' (n. 17 = 'Die Sprache' 1950 in *Unterwegs zur Sprache*) but in his 'living of mortals in the speaking of language' avoided returning explicitly to rhetoric. Question: 'What did Heidegger win, what did he lose, in doing this?'

Gadamer's response — the *political* turn (book p. 55): 'Later, a certain distance appeared (between us) due to his political mistake.' 'He erred when he did this. Still, a deficiency in the handling of his case is that no one said clearly, what I, however, say at every opportunity: He was the sole university president who occupied a German professorial chair, and who did not retain his presidency for even one year.' This is Gadamer's defense-of-Heidegger-against-political-cancellation.

Kemmann: 'Did his retreat out of politics contribute to his neglect of nonpoetic forms of speaking?' Gadamer: 'Yes, I believe so. ... poetic interpretation was his weakest area.' (book p. 56) — Gadamer concedes that Heidegger's later poetics-only stance was a real lacuna.
Bröcker poetry anecdote: Heidegger arrived at Walter Bröcker's with 'his poetic attempts'; Bröcker said 'Oh yes, that. The fire is over there.' 'And Heidegger was not offended by this!'

Kemmann pivots (book p. 57) to the SS 1924 *pathē* doctrine (n. 18 = GA 18, 117): 'how *logos* had its ground in *pathē*. The *pathē* are "the fundamental possibilities, by which Dasein primarily orients itself, is attuned". The possibility to speak about things is first presented within the so-characterized attunement [*Sich-Befindens*] and being-in-the-world, to the extent that the appearance, which the thing has in its immediate environment, has been removed' (n. 19 = GA 18, 262). 'Greek ontology also took its beginning from a *pathos*. ("The discussion of the being of beings out of a fear that it will at some point no longer be.")' (n. 20 = GA 18, 289).
Kemmann's question: 'In this context what is the meaning of characterizing *pathē* as "ground" and "fundamental possibilities"?'

Gadamer: 'That is the distrust of speaking. So speaking *is* not the first! There is still something, which ... therefore, one makes a decision about something without at the same time being able to say it to others. In this way one can, so to speak, justify what Heidegger said. It makes good sense to say that.' (book p. 57)

Kemmann presses: do *pathē* have *argumentative power*? 'It almost sounds like the *pathē* are a final judge — if one reversed the path and from *logos* returned to *pathos*.' Gadamer answers: 'Yes, but with the caveat that it is also — warranted [*bewährt*]. It is not simply a game. This circumstance then leads him to *logos*. I remember how he said, "*logos*," and I was completely puzzled that it should mean "language" and not "reason." I was completely puzzled, but then over and again it became very clear.' (book p. 57) The bewährt-caveat protects pathos from collapsing into pure-relativism while keeping its grounding role.

Decisive thesis: 'logos is able to express something in such a way that what is really intended is transferred to the other. And yet every logos is in some manner incomplete. That was decisive, I believe, also for Heidegger.' (book p. 57) — *every logos is incomplete* is Gadamer's hermeneutic adage at its source.

Kemmann turns to *Betroffensein* (being-affected): 'Nevertheless must not a being-affected [*Betroffensein*] already exist, before one can speak about it?' Gadamer: 'There is no doubt that Heidegger saw that. I mean, my own accomplishment beyond him, if one may call it that at all, goes exactly in this direction!' (book p. 57-58) — Gadamer self-locates: his hermeneutics extends beyond Heidegger by foregrounding *Betroffensein* as pre-linguistic ground.

Kemmann turns to fear (n. 22 = GA 18, 261): 'When we feel uncanny we begin to speak.' Gadamer: 'this is said in slight mockery' — but the genuine residue is 'the avoidance of the uncanny itself ... what is meant by the uncanny is the lifelong question concerning the afterlife. Fear is fear of death!' Yet 'fear, I believe, is not his last word.' (book p. 58)

Heidegger's last visit anecdote (book p. 58): 'On the day I saw him for the last time, I still remember that he came toward me in the yard, taking his wife's arm. Five days later he was dead, or eight days, I cannot remember. We were actually very cheerful. ... how he came, guided by his wife's arm, moved me very deeply. That was anything but a hiding from one's own fear. No, it was more, but fear always played a part in Heidegger.'

Gadamer's own turn to *ignoramus* (book p. 59): 'I conclude: *ignoramus* is our function. ... we cannot understand them any differently than as we, as all humans, similarly deal with all cases of destruction.'

Kemmann: 'How do you yourself see the relationship between linguisticality and attunement [*Befindlichkeit*]?' Gadamer's answer (book p. 59): '*Pathei mathos* (n. 24 = Aeschylus, *Agamemnon*, 177) is the decisive statement. One learns through experience. ... in life we do not relate to ourselves according to epistemological perspectives; rather we must live our own experiences.'

Gadamer expands: 'writing plays in the modern world, and now even in all other forms of reproduction. How can one actually communicate what is common, when such an apparatus stands in between? You understand a letter is something completely different than when you understand someone who is a partner in a conversation.' Conversation > writing.

Kemmann (book p. 59): SS 1924 says 'in fact the body participates in the genesis of *pathē*' (n. 25 = GA 18, 203). And Gadamer to Grondin (n. 26 = 'Die Logik des verbum interius', 30): 'pointing ... is also already language and the whole body speaks too, the language of gesture, the language of intonation, and so on. Linguisticality is only an approximating concept. One must go much, much further.'

Gadamer: 'As far as it is at all possible! One can even speak by being silent. That was also one of Heidegger's favorite problems. He said being silent is speaking.' (book p. 59-60) — Heidegger on silence-as-speaking.

Kemmann: 'Then what does linguisticality [*Sprachlichkeit*] mean?' Gadamer (book p. 60): 'Everything that can allow something to be understood. Therefore, hermeneutics; thereby its indefinability. ... It is much more important how one moves within linguisticality and that one is always prepared to seek new possibilities that allow the other to speak and that allow you to comprehend what he wished to say.' Then: 'No one who expresses something says what he really means. Because no one can ever have the last word, everything that one says only tends in a particular direction. ... In truth, rhetoric is the overarching concept for everything that has to do with the other.' This is the section's signature claim.

Kemmann (n. 27 = GA 18, 165): Heidegger says interaction with *pathē* is 'a question of *hexis*: "*Ethos* and *pathē* are constitutive of *legein* itself."' To Grondin (n. 28 = 'Dialogischer Rückblick', 292): 'the old, honorable concept of rhetoric' = the Plato *Statesman* sense, 'to know how to find the right word at the right moment.' This requires *dynamis* per Heidegger (n. 29 = GA 18, 118): 'To be able to see what speaks for a thing.'

Kemmann: 'What relationship does the rhetorical *dynamis* have to the human ability to understand?' Gadamer: 'It is the same *dynamis*!' (book p. 60) — the strongest single-sentence statement of Gadamer's identification of rhetorical dynamis with hermeneutic understanding.

Gadamer expands (book p. 60): 'one only speaks about understanding when it is not obvious. ... I emphasize this so much, because this is the way we come to understand one another! It consists first in just listening to the other and considering whether he couldn't perhaps also be correct.' Listening + admitting other's potential rightness = the constitutive moment of hermeneutic understanding.

Kemmann: 'What is the status of knowing in rhetoric? Is it *technē* or *phronēsis*?' Gadamer (book p. 61): 'In experience one does not know how to hold these apart. They are intertwined. ... *Phronēsis* is a whole virtue; it is not an ability, but a being, as Heidegger correctly stated. I mean, it is just a fact about *phronēsis* that one in fact can hardly say, "That is *phronēsis*!" One notices much more easily when it is lacking.' Phronēsis as virtue-not-ability is a specifically Aristotelian claim Gadamer attributes to Heidegger's correct reading.

Final political turn (book p. 61). Kemmann (n. 30 = 'Dialogischer Rückblick', 295): Aristotle 'placed [rhetoric] as a *technē* within politics' — does freeing rhetoric from this yield 'too much rhetoric or surrendering it to complete relativity'? 'Does rhetoric need to be tied to politics?'

Gadamer (book p. 61): 'Well, you cannot say that in general. ... already both are there. I am tempted to go into that, yet I must [see the limitations]. And if one does not achieve this perspective that includes both, then politics will just not become politics, but something that is the opposite of politics: that one knows everything ahead of time. The politics that one wanted as politics turns out not to be one. Rather, politics is exactly what one instinctively does and that then takes effect by itself.'

Kemmann: 'A philosophical rhetoric would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political.' Gadamer: 'That is it.' (book pp. 61-62) — *the* concise formula for the rhetoric-politics relation.

Closing remarks (book p. 62). On Gadamer's first-five-years-of-life thesis: language-acquisition is 'the colossal power of learning to speak — it is the building of the world!' On English-as-commerce: 'But there will be mother tongues everywhere. And that is what we must fight for. Every language has a new point of view.'

Closing (book p. 62): 'But surely it is true that rhetoric is, by far, not yet a possible word for what it itself is. In the end it is a communal listening. That is what my hermeneutics always had in view: there is no last, definitive word. That is given to no one. If the other misunderstands me, then I must speak differently until he understands me. We are all always only underway.' Then 'Professor Gadamer, thank you very much for this conversation.' — closing ceremonial frame.
Gadamer's titular conjunction *Sprachlichkeit* + rhetoric resolves into: rhetoric = communal listening; hermeneutics = the perpetual underway-ness of speaking-toward-the-other.
section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_structure: elaborate Q&A architecture in which Kemmann repeatedly stages an SS 1924 quotation and asks Gadamer to interpret; Gadamer responds with biographical-philosophical anecdotes that draw out the philosophical thesis from a personal memory; the section's signature is the convergence of *dynamis* (rhetoric) with *Sprachlichkeit* (hermeneutics) on the formula 'It is the same *dynamis*!'

section_3_key_concepts.name: Rhetoric as dynamis
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotle's *Rhetoric* I.2 defines rhetoric as a *dynamis* (power, capacity) belonging to being-human, not as a *technē* (art, craft). Gadamer follows Heidegger's GA 18, 114 dictum that the *technē*-designation 'is incorrect, whereas *dynamis* is the correct definition.' Rhetoric so defined is universal — 'everyone is a speaker' (book p. 49) — and grounds the human ability to understand: 'It is the same *dynamis*!' (book p. 60). The *dynamis*-reading aligns rhetoric with the hermeneutic *being able* (Wahrheit und Methode) rather than with poetic-or-craft production (*technē*).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Linguisticality
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's titular concept for Section IV. *Sprachlichkeit* names the medium in which 'mortals live in the speaking of language' (n. 17, citing 'Die Sprache' 1950). It is *not* nominalistically reducible to words: 'pointing ... is also already language and the whole body speaks too, the language of gesture, the language of intonation' (book p. 59, citing his Grondin conversation, n. 26). Sprachlichkeit's definition is 'everything that can allow something to be understood. Therefore, hermeneutics; thereby its indefinability' (book p. 60). 'Linguisticality is only an approximating concept. One must go much, much further' (book p. 59).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Logos as speaking (not reason)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's foundational realization at his first private Aristotle seminar with Heidegger (1923-24, Freiburg): '*logos* has something to do with speaking. In Marburg's Neo-Kantianism logos was just "reason."' (book p. 47) The Marburg-Neo-Kantian *logos = ratio* equation is the doctrine Heidegger broke for Gadamer; Heidegger's *logos = legein* (speaking, articulating) restores rhetoric's claim on the philosophical center. Gadamer recapitulates the breakthrough at p. 57: 'I remember how he said, "logos," and I was completely puzzled that it should mean "language" and not "reason." I was completely puzzled, but then over and again it became very clear.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: Pathē as ground of logos
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: pathē/passions as fundamental possibilities of orientation
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Following Heidegger SS 1924 (n. 18 = GA 18, 117): 'how logos had its ground in pathē. The pathē are "the fundamental possibilities, by which Dasein primarily orients itself, is attuned."' Pathē here are not affective add-ons to cognition but the *prior* attunement (*Sich-Befinden*) that makes speaking-about-things possible at all. Gadamer reads this as 'the distrust of speaking. So speaking is not the first! There is still something, which ... therefore, one makes a decision about something without at the same time being able to say it to others.' (book p. 57) Pathē is 'warranted [*bewährt*]. It is not simply a game' (p. 57) — it has argumentative power not via rational demonstration but via the witness of being-affected.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Sich-Befinden / Befindlichkeit
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's SS 1924 term (n. 19 = GA 18, 262, citing GA 18, 117) for 'the so-characterized attunement [*Sich-Befindens*] and being-in-the-world, to the extent that the appearance, which the thing has in its immediate environment, has been removed.' Kemmann translates Sich-Befinden into 'how one feels [im Befinden]' on book p. 57. The pre-BT form *Sich-Befinden* is the rhetorical-existential precursor to BT §29 *Befindlichkeit*. Gadamer treats the two as synonymous in the interview's idiom and identifies them with the pre-linguistic ground of speaking.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Being-affected
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's term for the pre-linguistic moment Kemmann brings into focus at book p. 57: 'Nevertheless must not a being-affected [*Betroffensein*] already exist, before one can speak about it?' Gadamer affirms: 'There is no doubt that Heidegger saw that. I mean, my own accomplishment beyond him, if one may call it that at all, goes exactly in this direction!' Betroffensein names the moment of being-claimed-by-something that *precedes* its articulation in logos. Gadamer locates his own hermeneutic advance over Heidegger here: foregrounding the *pre-articulate being-affected* as the ground that conversation must answer to.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Pathei mathos
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The Aeschylean adage Gadamer invokes (n. 24) at the question 'How do you yourself see the relationship between linguisticality and attunement [*Befindlichkeit*]?': '*Pathei mathos* is the decisive statement. One learns through experience. ... I have only recalled this statement because one always views it from epistemological points of view. But in life we do not relate to ourselves according to epistemological perspectives; rather we must live our own experiences.' (book p. 59) Pathei mathos couples pathos (the affective-existential ground) with mathēsis (learning) without an epistemological intermediary — i.e., without converting experience into propositional knowledge. The adage seals Gadamer's defense of Heidegger's pathē-doctrine against epistemological objections.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Conversation [Reden / Gespräch]
section_3_key_concepts.german_form: Reden, Gespräch (Diskussion is rejected as Latin)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's privileged mode of speaking: 'For this reason I elevate conversation, since in a conversation one immediately reacts to the offer. A conversation is able to bring both sides closer to one another. One has not just defended one's own position but has also understood the other.' (book p. 54) The Heidegger-contrast is structural: 'It was very difficult to speak with Heidegger because he wanted to understand step by step. So he did not terribly much like to discuss with me.' (book p. 50) Gadamer's hermeneutics is forged in this contrast: the *Gespräch* form, against the *Vortrag* (lecture) form, is what makes truth communicative. *Diskussion* (Latin) is rejected: 'I can say what I want, but it is, of course, just Latin' (book p. 52).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Phronēsis as virtue (not ability)
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: practical wisdom as virtue not ability
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Closing-section thesis (book p. 61): '*Phronēsis* is a whole virtue; it is not an ability, but a being, as Heidegger correctly stated.' The *technē/dynamis* dispute (Section II) is here completed by a parallel *technē/phronēsis* distinction: phronēsis is *hexis* (a settled disposition/being) rather than a *capacity-to-do*. Gadamer attributes the reading to Heidegger's correct interpretation; the SS 1923 phronēsis seminar in Freiburg (book p. 48) was the seedbed. The phronēsis-as-virtue claim secures the link from rhetoric (as dynamis) to ethics (phronēsis as hexis) without making rhetoric a *technē*.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Communal listening / Hermeneutics
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's hermeneutics is here defined twice. (i) Origin: 'Plato's Symposium ... where Socrates is told, "You will not understand what I will now say." Isn't it the truth? [laughs] — Well, that's the origin of my hermeneutics' (book p. 48). (ii) Closing definition: 'But surely it is true that rhetoric is, by far, not yet a possible word for what it itself is. In the end it is a communal listening. That is what my hermeneutics always had in view: there is no last, definitive word. That is given to no one. If the other misunderstands me, then I must speak differently until he understands me. We are all always only underway.' (book p. 62) Hermeneutics so defined is the practice of finite-but-perpetual speaking-toward-understanding; rhetoric is its proper name *and* its insufficient name.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Speaking-to-others
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: From Heidegger's SS 1924 (n. 8 = GA 18, 169f): 'I only wish to point out that it might be more appropriate if philosophers could decide to consider what speaking to others really means.' Gadamer's frame: philosophers *lose sight* of speaking-to-others (Marburg-Freiburg targets: Kroner, Hartmann, secondarily Husserl). Heidegger's pedagogical ideal (n. 13 = GA 63, 327): 'to speak to another, approach the other in the manner of communicating. The actual being of a teacher is: to stand before an other and to speak to him, and in such a way that the other, listening, follows him.' Gadamer's reading: this defines being-a-teacher *constitutively* through the listening-following relation. The structural significance: *Mitsein* in BT §26 is fueled by exactly this rhetorical-pedagogical scene.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Every logos is incomplete
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's thesis at book p. 57: '*Logos* is able to express something in such a way that what is really intended is transferred to the other. And yet every logos is in some manner incomplete. That was decisive, I believe, also for Heidegger.' Logos's expressive power is real but never closed; this incompleteness is structural (not contingent failure) and grounds the perpetual *underway-ness* of conversation (book p. 62 close). The thesis aligns Gadamer's reading with Heidegger's emphatically and resists any attempt to convert hermeneutic finitude into pure relativism — pathē are bewährt; logos is incomplete; conversation is the only path.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Heidegger as rhetor (vs. as conversationalist)
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: Heidegger the lecturer was rhetorically masterful but anti-conversational
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The titular concept. Gadamer testifies: 'Heidegger's manner of lecturing was already enormously fascinating — oh yes, rhetorically masterful! ... had an enormous radiance. We were all awestruck!' (book p. 50) But: 'It was very difficult to speak with Heidegger because he wanted to understand step by step. ... He didn't like that; he needed the steps. ... it was not a conversation. ... It was not an exchange with the audience.' (book pp. 50-51) Gadamer thus *splits* Heidegger's rhetorical practice: as orator/teacher, supreme; as conversation-partner, refused. The titular 'Heidegger as Rhetor' captures only half of what rhetoric (in Gadamer's mature sense) requires; the other half — communal listening — Heidegger did not develop.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Heidegger's political mistake
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's careful formulation (book p. 55): 'a certain distance appeared (between us) due to his political mistake and the way he nevertheless played along, understandably so, for a little bit. However, everybody who was not blind must have known. He erred when he did this. Still, a deficiency in the handling of his case is that no one said clearly, what I, however, say at every opportunity: He was the sole university president who occupied a German professorial chair, and who did not retain his presidency for even one year.' Gadamer concedes the error but *defends* against the cancellation-by-default move; his defense is brief, factual, and acknowledges the seriousness of the error without deriving Heidegger's whole thought from it. Footnote 31 cites Gadamer's own 'Über die politische Inkompetenz der Philosophie' (Hermeneutische Entwürfe 2000).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Rhetoric and politics binding
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: rhetoric and politics binding (the proper relation)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's closing thesis-question, in response to Kemmann: 'A philosophical rhetoric would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political' (book p. 61-62). Aristotle, per Kemmann, 'placed [rhetoric] as a *technē* within politics' (n. 30); Gadamer holds that freeing rhetoric from this *technē*-status while keeping rhetoric political-aware is the right balance. Politics that knows everything in advance ceases to be politics: 'politics is exactly what one instinctively does and that then takes effect by itself' (book p. 61). The phronēsis-as-virtue thesis (above) supplies the structural reason: rhetoric, like phronēsis, is a being not an instrument; it pertains to politics without being reducible to political instrumentation.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Energeia / dynamis pairing
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: From Section II response (book p. 49): 'Heidegger was still using *technē*, until he began emphatically using the concept of *energeia*. And so he associated the concept of *dynamis* with the concept of *energeia*, and missed the other one.' Gadamer reads Heidegger's eventual *Met. IX* register (energeia ↔ dynamis) as the framework that *displaced* the technē-rhetoric register but at a cost: the productive/poietic dimension of technē was 'missed.' This is a subtle correction of Heidegger by Gadamer himself.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Hexis (ethos and pathē constitutive of legein)
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: settled disposition; ethos and passions are constitutive of speaking
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Kemmann's framing at book p. 60 (n. 27 = GA 18, 165): 'The interaction with the *pathē*, Heidegger says, is a question of *hexis*: "*Ethos* and *pathē* are constitutive of *legein* itself."' Hexis is the disposition that holds ethos+pathē together as the standing-condition of speaking; this is the operational link between Aristotle's *Rhetoric* II (pathē-doctrine) and the SS 1924 thesis that rhetoric is the hermeneutic of Dasein. Gadamer accepts the framework without expansion (the question moves immediately to the rhetorical-dynamis question).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Saying what the Ancients meant (philological aim)
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: philological aim of the SS 1924 lecture
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: From Heidegger SS 1924 (n. 10 = GA 18, 3 plus n. 12 = GA 63, 329; n. 13 = GA 63, 327): 'The lecture does not aim at something philosophical. It concerns the understanding of basic concepts in their conceptuality. The aim is philological and is to practice somewhat more the reading of philosophers.' Plus the concluding sentence: 'What is at stake is not to say something new, but to say what the Ancients really meant.' Gadamer reads the opening as defensive self-frame ('not to fall into the warranted suspicion that he just wanted to push his own views' — book p. 53) but the closing as 'his colossal demand.' The philological aim is genuine and binding; it organizes the entire SS 1924 lecture's mode and constrains how Aristotle's rhetoric must be read.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Rhetoric as overarching concept
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: rhetoric as overarching concept for everything that has to do with the other
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's signature claim at book p. 60: 'In truth, rhetoric is the overarching concept for everything that has to do with the other.' This subsumes hermeneutics-as-Sprachlichkeit under rhetoric (rather than the reverse) at the level of a name; in the earlier conversation with Kühne-Bertram & Rodi (n. 5) he had defended 'the very broad concept of rhetoric ... that contained all the humanities until modern times.' The thesis sets up the closing identification 'rhetoric ... is, by far, not yet a possible word for what it itself is. In the end it is a communal listening' (p. 62). Rhetoric is *the* word *and* an insufficient word — both at once.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Silence as speaking
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Gadamer's report (book pp. 59-60): 'One can even speak by being silent. That was also one of Heidegger's favorite problems. He said being silent is speaking ... that even being silent is speaking. He liked that a lot, already in Marburg.' The Heideggerian thesis (cf. BT §34 *Schweigen*) is taken up appreciatively by Gadamer to extend the Sprachlichkeit-thesis: linguisticality includes *not-speaking* as a mode of speaking, broadening the rhetorical field to embrace silence, gesture, intonation, body — everything Grondin-conversation (n. 26) listed.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Aristotle's *Rhetoric* I.2 defines rhetoric correctly as *dynamis* (a power belonging to being-human), not as *technē* (an art); Heidegger's SS 1924 lecture established this reading and Gadamer continues to hold it in 1999-2001.
premises: Aristotle Rhet. 1.2 supplies the *dynamis* definition.
Aristotle himself elsewhere designates rhetoric as *technē*; Heidegger's GA 18, 114 says this 'designation is incorrect.'
Rhetoric-as-dynamis is universal: 'everyone is a speaker' (book p. 49).
*Dynamis* aligns rhetoric with being-able rather than with productive-poietic craft.
targets: The rhetorical tradition that took *technē* as the core (Aristotle's own elsewhere-designation; the post-Aristotelian tradition Kemmann mentions in II opening).
Marburg Neo-Kantianism's reduction of *logos* to *ratio* (book p. 47).
Any reading that makes rhetoric a tool rather than a constitutive human capacity.

section_4_main_positions.claim: *Logos* in Heidegger's SS 1924 reading is *speaking* (legein), not reason (ratio); this discovery is the seed of Gadamer's hermeneutics.
premises: Marburg Neo-Kantianism (Cohen, Natorp, Hartmann) reduced logos to reason.
Heidegger's private Aristotle seminar in Freiburg 1923 taught Gadamer the legein-reading directly.
The 1923 phronēsis seminar reinforced the practical-rhetorical sense of logos.
The SS 1924 GA 18 thesis 'logos had its ground in pathē' (n. 18) extends the legein-reading by making logos's ground pre-cognitive and affective.
targets: Marburg Neo-Kantianism's logos = reason (book p. 47).
Any rationalist reduction of speaking to thinking.

section_4_main_positions.claim: *Pathē* are 'fundamental possibilities by which Dasein primarily orients itself, is attuned' (GA 18, 117); they are the *ground* of *logos* and have argumentative power that is *bewährt* (warranted) — neither final-judge nor mere game.
premises: Heidegger SS 1924 (GA 18, 117, 262, 289) establishes pathē as ground of speaking.
Greek ontology itself begins from a pathos: 'discussion of the being of beings out of a fear that it will at some point no longer be' (GA 18, 289).
Speaking is not 'first': '*Sich-Befinden*' precedes articulation.
But pathos is *bewährt* — warranted, not arbitrary; this protects the thesis from collapse into pure-affective relativism.
*Betroffensein* (being-affected) is the pre-articulate condition Gadamer claims as his own advance beyond Heidegger.
targets: Epistemological framings that make pathē mere objects of cognition (book p. 59 'in life we do not relate to ourselves according to epistemological perspectives').
Interpretations that read Heidegger's pathē-doctrine as collapsing logos into affective irrationalism.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Every logos is incomplete; understanding requires perpetual conversation; rhetoric/hermeneutics is communal listening, not a final-word capacity.
premises: Logos can transfer what is intended, but is structurally incomplete (book p. 57).
'No one who expresses something says what he really means. ... no one can ever have the last word' (book p. 60).
Understanding is *consideration* of whether the other 'couldn't perhaps also be correct' (book p. 60).
Hermeneutics so understood originated for Gadamer in Plato's Symposium 'You will not understand' (book p. 48).
targets: Methodological rationalism that demands closure of meaning.
Pure-relativism that abandons logos's communicative function.

section_4_main_positions.claim: The rhetorical *dynamis* is the same *dynamis* as the human ability to understand: 'It is the same dynamis!' (book p. 60).
premises: Rhetoric is *dynamis* (P1).
Linguisticality (*Sprachlichkeit*) is the medium of understanding.
Hexis pulls *ethos* + *pathē* together as constitutive of *legein* (n. 27 = GA 18, 165).

The 'old, honorable concept of rhetoric' (Plato Statesman: 'know how to find the right word at the right moment', n. 28) requires the *dynamis* that GA 18, 118 names: 'To be able to see what speaks for a thing' (n. 29).
targets: Any technical/instrumental reading of rhetoric as a sub-domain of skill.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's pedagogy was rhetorically masterful but anti-conversational; Gadamer's hermeneutics was forged in this contrast — privileging *Gespräch* (conversation) over *Vortrag* (lecture).
premises: Heidegger's lectures were 'rhetorically masterful', awe-inducing (book p. 50).
Heidegger 'did not terribly much like to discuss' with Gadamer; he 'wanted to understand step by step' (book p. 50).
'It was not an exchange with the audience' (book p. 51); even with Gadamer himself the conversational form was refused.
Yet Heidegger's stated pedagogical ideal (n. 13 = GA 63, 327) defined teaching constitutively through speaking-toward-the-other-such-that-the-other-listening-follows-him.
Gadamer extended the SS 1924 thesis by privileging conversation: 'A conversation is able to bring both sides closer to one another' (book p. 54).
targets: The Heidegger-as-monological-orator picture that Gadamer himself partially affirms but then qualifies.
Rhetorical ostentation without substance (Eugen Kühnemann at Breslau, 'ghastly', n. 14).

section_4_main_positions.claim: *Sprachlichkeit* is the medium 'in which mortals live in the speaking of language' and its definition is 'everything that can allow something to be understood. Therefore, hermeneutics; thereby its indefinability' (book p. 60). Linguisticality includes silence, gesture, intonation, body.
premises: Later Heidegger ('Die Sprache' 1950, n. 17) articulated 'mortals live in the speaking of language' but distanced himself from a nominalistic philosophy of language.
Heidegger SS 1924 (GA 18, 203) said 'in fact the body participates in the genesis of pathē' (n. 25).
Gadamer to Grondin (n. 26): 'pointing ... is also already language and the whole body speaks too. Linguisticality is only an approximating concept. One must go much, much further.'
Heidegger's 'silence is speaking' thesis is endorsed by Gadamer as a Sprachlichkeit-extension.
targets: Nominalistic philosophy of language that reduces meaning to word-tokens.
Any thesis that makes silence the absence of speaking rather than a mode of it.

section_4_main_positions.claim: *Pathei mathos* (Aeschylus, Agamemnon 177) is 'the decisive statement' on the relationship between linguisticality and attunement: we learn through experience, not epistemologically.
premises: Heidegger's SS 1924 pathē-doctrine grounds logos in pathē (P3).
Aeschylus *Agamemnon* 177's *pathei mathos* couples pathos with mathēsis without epistemological intermediary.
'In life we do not relate to ourselves according to epistemological perspectives; rather we must live our own experiences' (book p. 59).
Hermeneutics so understood is not a method but the lived form of being-Dasein.
targets: Epistemological readings of hermeneutics (Hirsch, methodological objectivism — implicit).
Reductions of experience to propositional knowledge.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger erred politically (Nazism); the deficiency of his case is also visible in his retreat from non-poetic forms of speaking — a poetics-only stance that abandoned rhetorical-political engagement.
premises: Heidegger 'erred when he did this' (the rectorate); the political mistake created distance between Heidegger and Gadamer (book p. 55).
Heidegger occupied his rectorate for less than a year — a fact Gadamer insists on stating 'at every opportunity' (book p. 55).

The political retreat coincided with Heidegger's poetics-only turn (Hölderlin, Trakl): 'Concerning poetic forms of speaking, he just had such a trust in his own philosophical fantasy that he did not consider the other forms worthwhile' (book p. 56).
'Poetic interpretation was his weakest area' (book p. 56) — Bröcker anecdote.
Footnote 31 cites Gadamer's own 'Über die politische Inkompetenz der Philosophie' (Hermeneutische Entwürfe 2000).
targets: Pure-cancellation moves that derive Heidegger's whole thought from the Nazi episode.
The view that Heidegger's later poetics is the proper completion of his early thought (Gadamer holds it as a *retreat*).

section_4_main_positions.claim: A philosophical rhetoric 'would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political' (book p. 61-62); rhetoric and politics are bound but rhetoric must not be reduced to political *technē*.
premises: Aristotle 'placed [rhetoric] as a technē within politics' (per Kemmann's gloss, n. 30) — but rhetoric-as-technē is the *incorrect* designation (P1).
Phronēsis is a virtue not an ability (book p. 61); it is a 'whole virtue' / a 'being'.
Politics that knows everything in advance ceases to be politics: 'politics is exactly what one instinctively does and that then takes effect by itself' (book p. 61).
If rhetoric were absorbed into the political, one could not 'achieve an understanding of what politics is' (book p. 61).
targets: Aristotle's own elsewhere-placement of rhetoric within politics-as-technē.
Modern instrumentalizations of rhetoric as political tool.
Anti-political philosophical purism (the opposite extreme).

section_4_main_positions.claim: [POSITIONED INTERLOCUTOR — KEMMANN]: The interview's italicized questions stake an analytical position — that the *technē/dynamis* alternative is itself the question; that the *pathē*-as-ground claim demands attention to argumentative power; that Heidegger's 'living of mortals in the speaking of language' (1950) is in tension with his neglect of rhetoric; and that a philosophical rhetoric 'would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political.'
premises: Kemmann frames each section by Heidegger-quotation + analytical question.
Section II's pivotal question 'What is at stake in this alternative (technē/dynamis)?' is Kemmann's framing, not Gadamer's.
Section IV's *pathē-as-final-judge?* and the *Betroffensein-as-prior-to-speaking?* questions force the conversation toward Gadamer's positive-proposal terrain.

Kemmann's closing summary 'A philosophical rhetoric would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political' (book p. 62) is a *position-statement* affirmed by Gadamer's 'That is it.'
targets: Implicit: any reading of Heidegger that bypasses the SS 1924 lecture's rhetorical-philological aim.
Implicit: any reading of Gadamer that does not connect his hermeneutics to the rhetorical-dynamis tradition.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Aristotle
section_5_interlocutors.role: primary text-source; rhetoric I.2 (dynamis), Rhetoric II (pathē), De partibus animalium (Scheler-correction anecdote), the phronēsis seminar of SS 1923
citations: Rhetoric 1.2 (rhetoric as dynamis) — book p. 49; foundational
Rhetoric II (pathē-doctrine, especially fear) — implicit in 'pathē as ground of logos'
De partibus animalium (the typo-correction anecdote) — book p. 52-53
phronēsis (NE VI, 1923 seminar) — book p. 48; book p. 61 ('phronēsis is a whole virtue')
Plato Statesman (Aristotle implicit; Plato source) — book p. 60 ('right word at the right moment', n. 28)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: borrowed: the *dynamis*-definition is the volume's central rhetoric-claim; the pathē-doctrine grounds logos; phronēsis as virtue-not-ability binds rhetoric to ethics. Gadamer treats Aristotle as the master text and Heidegger as the master interpreter.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Plato
section_5_interlocutors.role: second classical authority; *Symposium* origin of Gadamer's hermeneutics; *Statesman* on the right word at the right moment
citations: Symposium last phase ('You will not understand what I will now say') — book p. 48; explicitly 'the origin of my hermeneutics'
Statesman ('how to find the right word at the right moment') — book p. 60, via Grondin n. 28
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: borrowed: Plato Symposium is the seed of hermeneutic finitude; Plato Statesman supplies the kairos-of-speech that links rhetoric to phronēsis.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Cicero & Quintilian
section_5_interlocutors.role: Roman rhetorical tradition; Gadamer's classical-philology study material
citations: Cicero (read with Lommatzsch for Latin practice) — book p. 48
Quintilian (the late rhetoric Gadamer specialized in) — book p. 48
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: biographical-formative: Cicero/Quintilian gave Gadamer the late-rhetoric register that he 'delved further' into 'because rhetoric was closest to philosophy'; this background shaped his readiness for Heidegger's rhetorical Aristotle.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Aeschylus
section_5_interlocutors.role: tragic-poetic source for *pathei mathos*
citations: Agamemnon 177 (pathei mathos) — book p. 59, n. 24
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: borrowed: pathei mathos is 'the decisive statement' on linguisticality-attunement relation.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
section_5_interlocutors.role: the interview's subject; Gadamer's teacher 1923-24, intellectual antagonist 1933+, lifelong interlocutor
citations: Phänomenologische Interpretationen zu Aristoteles ('Natorp Report' 1922; Dilthey-Jahrbuch 6, 1989) — n. 1, the essay that secured Heidegger's Marburg call

Grundbegriffe der aristotelischen Philosophie (SS 1924) = GA 18 — n. 7 (114), n. 8 (169f), n. 10 (3), n. 16 (117), n. 18 (177 — pathē as fundamental possibilities), n. 19 (262), n. 20 (289), n. 21, n. 22 (261), n. 25 (203), n. 27 (165), n. 29 (118)
Ontologie. Hermeneutik der Faktizität = GA 63 (SS 1923) — n. 10 implicit, n. 12 (329), n. 13 (327)
Metaphysische Anfangsgründe der Logik = GA 26 — n. 9 (Scheler obituary)
'Die Sprache' (1950) in Unterwegs zur Sprache — n. 17
Sein und Zeit (the political reading; the 'Heidegger erred' context) — book p. 55
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: primary subject; Gadamer is at once witness, student, and corrector — affirming the SS 1924 rhetorical Aristotle, conceding the political failure, supplementing the pathos-doctrine with *Betroffensein*.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Paul Natorp
section_5_interlocutors.role: Marburg Neo-Kantian; Heidegger's elder colleague; logos = reason doctrine
citations: Natorp (recommended Heidegger to Marburg, n. 2; 'still had contact with him for another year and a half' after the call) — book pp. 47, 53
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Natorp's Neo-Kantianism is the logos = reason doctrine that Heidegger's logos = legein breaks. But Gadamer notes (book p. 53): 'we have not done enough with this, namely to understand the influence the later Natorp had on the younger Heidegger' — the genealogical line is more complicated than simple opposition.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Nicolai Hartmann
section_5_interlocutors.role: Marburg philosopher; aristocratic teacher; Heidegger-comparison foil
citations: Hartmann (recommended Heidegger to Marburg, n. 2; 'a knight — so aristocratic and reserved'; 'a wonderful relationship with his students' but 'successful teaching was clearly on Heidegger's side'; 'carefully read Aristotle' but it 'did not actually transfer to his own thinking') — book pp. 47, 49-50, 53
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Hartmann is the well-meaning Aristotle-reader whose reading 'did not actually transfer'; Heidegger is the contrast — Aristotle 'suddenly came alive' (book p. 50). Hartmann is also one of the philosophers Heidegger criticizes for losing-sight-of-speaking.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Edmund Husserl
section_5_interlocutors.role: Heidegger's teacher (Freiburg); phenomenology's founder
citations: Husserl ('he actually never tried to hide his admiration for Husserl, at least not at that time') — book p. 49

'He was not so sure himself how far he would come in his confrontation with Husserl. He naturally avoided this confrontation in Freiburg. There, for reasons of self-preservation, he fulfilled as best as possible the role that Husserl had allotted him. When he was in Marburg the situation was also difficult for him.' — book p. 53
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Husserl is Heidegger's phenomenological elder whom Heidegger eventually broke from; the rhetoric-route through Aristotle was Heidegger's way of moving past Husserl. Gadamer marks the Marburg-Freiburg location-difference as constitutive of Heidegger's strategic self-positioning.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Rudolf Bultmann
section_5_interlocutors.role: Marburg theologian; successful collaborator with Heidegger
citations: Bultmann ('I tried to bring the two together, but that failed completely, whereas it worked with Bultmann and Heidegger') — book p. 50
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted (positive): Bultmann is the case where Heidegger's pedagogy *did* engage another mind productively; the contrast with the failed Hartmann-Heidegger pairing illuminates Heidegger's selectivity.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Max Scheler
section_5_interlocutors.role: phenomenologist; Heidegger's critical foil; subject of the 1928 obituary anecdote
citations: Scheler (death May 19, 1928; obituary by Heidegger printed in Metaphysische Anfangsgründe der Logik = GA 26, n. 9) — book p. 52
The de partibus animae/animal typo-correction anecdote — book pp. 52-53
'Scheler is the only one besides Heidegger about whom I must say that his lectures were simply fascinating. He had a demonic radiance, very dramatic.' — book p. 52
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Scheler is the figure Heidegger's malice repeatedly attacked; Gadamer's narration of the typo-correction reveals both Heidegger's polemical intensity and his accomplishment in retracting publicly. The episode is itself a rhetorical lesson — in how a philosopher's combative speaking can be both excessive and recoverable.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Hannah Arendt
section_5_interlocutors.role: Heidegger's student and lover; 'an interesting, talented Jewess'; Heidegger's secret
citations: Arendt (the educated-by-Heidegger relationship and its secrecy; Jakob Klein's misjudgment) — book p. 50
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: biographical context: Arendt's hidden role illustrates Heidegger's ability to 'situate the other within his thinking' (book p. 51) — a remark Gadamer makes about Heidegger generally. The Arendt anecdote is the personal-illustration of Heidegger's rhetorical-pedagogical dominance.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Karl Löwith
section_5_interlocutors.role: Heidegger's student; later attacker, then reconciled
citations: Löwith ('just before Löwith died, [Heidegger] wrote him such a wonderful letter that Löwith and his wife were completely charmed') — book p. 51
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Löwith's case shows Heidegger's capacity for humane recovery — 'sanctioning Löwith's own path as a bold path' — even after public conflict.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Walter Bröcker
section_5_interlocutors.role: Heidegger's student and friend; the poetry-rejection anecdote
citations: Bröcker ('Oh yes, that. The fire is over there.' — Heidegger's poems anecdote) — book p. 56
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted (against Heidegger's poetics): the Bröcker anecdote secures Gadamer's claim that 'poetic interpretation was [Heidegger's] weakest area.'

section_5_interlocutors.name: Friedrich Hölderlin & Paul Celan
section_5_interlocutors.role: the poets Heidegger turned to in his later phase
citations: Celan ('the part he played with Celan — he is himself to be blamed. Although it grieved him and he was prepared for complete admiration. But — oh well.') — book p. 56
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Heidegger's later poetry-turn yielded mixed results; the Celan reference signals Gadamer's view that Heidegger was 'never quite in the right place. He saw only himself, reflected.' The poetic-turn parallels the political failure.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Eugen Kühnemann
section_5_interlocutors.role: Breslau professor; example of rhetorical-ostentation-without-substance
citations: Kühnemann ('it was ghastly') — book p. 54, n. 14
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Kühnemann is the negative example — 'too much rhetoric' — that throws the Heidegger 'much more substantive' assessment into relief.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Paul Friedländer
section_5_interlocutors.role: Gadamer's second philology teacher; Hellenism-Greek-Latin scholar
citations: Friedländer ('began to concern himself with topics from the time of Hellenism and to ask what was slowly developing between Latin and Greek') — book p. 48, n. 4
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: biographical-formative: Friedländer's Latin-Greek interface concern is the philological neighborhood Gadamer entered, predisposing him to Heidegger's anti-Latin pivot.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Ernst Lommatzsch
section_5_interlocutors.role: Gadamer's first philology teacher (Marburg); supplied Cicero
citations: Lommatzsch ('had given me Cicero to read so that I could practice my Latin') — book p. 48, n. 3
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: biographical-formative: Lommatzsch is the source of Gadamer's late-rhetoric (Cicero, Quintilian) competence.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Richard Kroner
section_5_interlocutors.role: Freiburg philosopher; named target of Heidegger's 'philosophers losing sight of speaking-to-others'
citations: Kroner (book p. 49) — paired with Hartmann as Heidegger's targets
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: contrasted: Kroner exemplifies the philosophical type Heidegger criticized — the rhetoric-blind academic philosopher.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Gudrun Kühne-Bertram & Frithjof Rodi
section_5_interlocutors.role: Gadamer's recent interview partners (Dilthey-Jahrbuch 1997-98)
citations: 'Die Logik des verbum interius: Hans-Georg Gadamer in Conversation with Gudrun Kühne-Bertram and Frithjof Rodi', Dilthey-Jahrbuch 11 (1997-98): 19-30, esp. 29 — n. 5; n. 26 (esp. 30)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: previous-statement source: the 'very broad concept of rhetoric' position Kemmann's question (book p. 48) is taken from this conversation; the body-as-speaking thesis (book p. 59) is taken from this conversation.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Jean Grondin
section_5_interlocutors.role: Gadamer's interview partner (Gadamer Lesebuch, 1997)
citations: 'Dialogischer Rückblick auf das Gesammelte Werk' in Gadamer Lesebuch (Mohr Siebeck, 1997), 280-295 — n. 6 (esp. 284); n. 28 (292); n. 30 (295)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: previous-statement source: the rhetoric-and-the-humanities thesis (book p. 48) is from this conversation; the Plato Statesman 'right word at the right moment' formula (book p. 60) is from this conversation; the closing question about freeing rhetoric from politics (book p. 61) is from this conversation.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Jakob Klein
section_5_interlocutors.role: Gadamer's friend; misjudged the Arendt-Heidegger relationship
citations: Klein ('that's totally crazy ... in such a small town everyone would know about it!') — book p. 50
section_5_interlocutors.relationship_to_argument: biographical-illustrative: Klein's misjudgment underscores Heidegger's success at maintaining secrecy — i.e., at controlling the audience-relation across multiple registers.

section_5_interlocutors.name: Mark Michalski

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Rhetoric-as-dynamis (Section II) vs. rhetoric-as-overarching-concept-for-everything-that-has-to-do-with-the-other (Section IV). The Section II claim narrows rhetoric to a specific Aristotelian definition (Rhet. I.2); the Section IV claim broadens rhetoric to subsume hermeneutics. The two claims are compatible *if* dynamis is the universal human capacity-for-speaking-and-understanding (P5 makes this explicit: 'It is the same dynamis!'), but the texture of each claim is different: II is doctrinal-philological; IV is hermeneutic-existential.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's resolution at book p. 60 ('It is the same dynamis!') makes the broad and narrow senses of rhetoric one capacity — the human dynamis of speaking-understanding. The narrowness of the I.2 definition is *protective* (against technē-instrumentalization); the breadth of Section IV is *expansive* (against nominalist reductions of language). Both are needed.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Heidegger-as-rhetorically-masterful-orator (book p. 50) vs. Heidegger-as-anti-conversational (book p. 50). 'Rhetorically masterful' applauds Heidegger's command of the lecture form; 'anti-conversational' criticizes him for refusing the *Gespräch* (the form rhetoric in Gadamer's mature sense properly takes). The titular 'Heidegger as Rhetor' captures only the former.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's hermeneutics is forged in this contrast. Heidegger had the rhetorical *dynamis* but did not develop its conversational-listening completion; Gadamer's lifelong project (Gespräch + communal listening + 'every logos is incomplete') is the corrective extension of what Heidegger left undone. The titular phrase 'Heidegger as Rhetor' is therefore both descriptive (he was) and incomplete (he was, but only one half of what rhetoric requires).

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Heidegger's political 'erring' (book p. 55) vs. Gadamer's defense ('he was the sole university president who occupied a German professorial chair, and who did not retain his presidency for even one year', p. 55). Gadamer affirms the error and yet limits its hermeneutic consequences. There is a tension between full acknowledgment of the political failure and the refusal to derive Heidegger's whole thought from it.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's position is principled but compressed: the political mistake is real (worth acknowledging 'at every opportunity'), but the case-handling-deficiency he points to is the failure of others to *factually* note the brevity of Heidegger's rectorate. The point is not exoneration but proportion. Footnote 31 directs to Gadamer's own 'Über die politische Inkompetenz der Philosophie' for the longer treatment. [INTERP-low: the compression of this discussion in the interview leaves a structural under-development; readers seeking a developed account must go to the cited essay.]

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: VT2 in volume terms: rhetoric as dynamis (Heidegger SS 1924, GA 18, 114; Gadamer endorsing) vs. rhetoric as technē (Aristotle's elsewhere-designation). Gadamer follows Heidegger in calling the technē-designation 'incorrect.' But Aristotle himself uses both. What philosophical work is being done by Heidegger's choice of dynamis-only?
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Heidegger's choice protects rhetoric from instrumentalization (technē as productive-craft) and aligns it with the human capacity-for-being. Gadamer endorses but adds a critical note (book p. 49): 'Heidegger was still using technē, until he began emphatically using the concept of energeia. And so he associated the concept of dynamis with the concept of energeia, and missed the other one.' The 'missed' technē-side is the productive-poietic dimension that the dynamis-energeia coupling does not reach. This is a subtle Gadamer-internal correction of Heidegger.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: VT3 in volume terms: Gadamer's testimony to the SS 1924 → BT continuity (the rhetorical Aristotle reading carried into hermeneutics-of-facticity → BT) vs. Pöggeler's restriction-thesis (Ch 7: post-1924 Heidegger abandons rhetoric for poetics/topology of being). Gadamer is on the continuity side, with the qualification that Heidegger himself drifted toward poetics (book p. 56) — so partial alignment with Pöggeler.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's testimony supports continuity at the level of GA 18 → SZ § 29 (rhetoric → Befindlichkeit/Mitsein) but acknowledges restriction at the level of post-1933 Heidegger (poetics-only as 'his weakest area'). Phase 3 should record Gadamer as continuity-with-late-restriction, not pure-continuity.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: VT5 in volume terms: pathos-as-cognitive-resource (Hyde's epideictic) vs. pathos-as-ontological-substrate (Gross). Gadamer's reading of pathē as 'fundamental possibilities' grounding logos (P3) sits closer to Gross's substrate-reading than to Hyde's deliberate-resource-reading; but Gadamer's *bewährt* ('warranted') caveat preserves the argumentative function pathē can perform — partial alignment with Hyde.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's pathos-doctrine occupies a productive middle: pathē are pre-articulate ground (Gross-side) but also bewährt grounds-for-judgment (Hyde-side). The bewährt caveat is the volume's most philosophically careful navigation of the cognitive-vs-ontological pathos dispute.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: VT6 in volume terms: Gross's 'hermeneutics displacing rhetoric is a substantive political-ethical loss' vs. Gadamer's apparent-softening that hermeneutics is the natural extension of rhetoric. Gadamer in the interview *partially affirms* Gross's worry: he concedes 'I no longer felt that I was at the apex of my philological knowledge' (book p. 62) and that he never held a class on rhetoric, but he also asserts 'In truth, rhetoric is the overarching concept for everything that has to do with the other' (book p. 60). The position is: hermeneutics *is* rhetoric properly understood, so there is no displacement at the conceptual level — but at the institutional-pedagogical level, Gadamer admits a displacement that Gross calls 'loss.'
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Gadamer's position is more nuanced than Gross suggests: at the conceptual level, rhetoric and hermeneutics are coextensive ('It is the same dynamis!'); at the institutional level, Gadamer acknowledges he did not develop a rhetoric pedagogy and that this was a real limitation. Phase 3 should record this as alignment with Gross's *institutional* loss claim and disagreement with the *conceptual* loss claim.

section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.description: Kemmann's italicized questions stake analytical positions (P11-Kemmann) that themselves frame the conversation. Section II's 'What is at stake in this alternative (technē/dynamis)?' is not Gadamer's but Kemmann's — and yet it organizes the entire discussion. The interview is therefore a *jointly-authored* analytical artifact, not a pure-Gadamer testimony.
section_8_tensions_and_open_questions.synthesis: Phase 2 records Kemmann's questions as positioned-interlocutor framings that contribute substantially to the essay's argumentative shape. The volume's editorial provenance (Kemmann is also a co-editor and bibliographer) makes his framings authoritative inputs to the volume's reading of Gadamer.

section_10_local_graph_edges.note: Aristotle's Rhetoric I.2 *is* the locus where rhetoric is defined as *dynamis* (1355b25ff., dynamis tou theorēsai). Gadamer (and Heidegger SS 1924) takes this as the correct definition.

Heidegger GA 18, 114 (quoted at p. 49): 'this designation [technē] is incorrect, whereas dynamis is the correct definition.' The dynamis/technē alternative is the volume's tension VT2, with this essay as the locus classicus.
Heidegger's GA 18, 114 *interprets* Aristotle's Rhetoric I.2: the *dynamis*-clause is to be retained, the *technē*-clause rejected. This is a reading-relation, philologically grounded.

'In Marburg's Neo-Kantianism logos was just "reason." ... I was completely puzzled that it should mean "language" and not "reason"' (book pp. 47, 57). The legein-vs-ratio dispute is at the doctrinal heart of the Heidegger-Gadamer relation.
Heidegger SS 1924 (GA 18, 117): 'logos had its ground in pathē.' Speaking presupposes the prior attunement (Sich-Befinden) of the speaker. Gadamer's reading at p. 57: 'speaking is not the first.'

GA 18, 117 ('logos had its ground in pathē; pathē are fundamental possibilities by which Dasein orients itself') is refined at GA 18, 262 ('possibility to speak ... presented within the so-characterized attunement [Sich-Befindens]'). The latter specifies the mode of attunement.

The pathē-as-ground claim is operationalized in Heidegger's *Sich-Befinden* (SS 1924, GA 18, 262) and *Befindlichkeit* (BT §29). Gadamer treats the two terms as synonymous; the BT term is the institutionalized form of the SS 1924 thesis.

Kemmann (p. 57): 'must not a being-affected [Betroffensein] already exist, before one can speak about it?' Gadamer affirms: 'There is no doubt that Heidegger saw that. I mean, my own accomplishment beyond him ... goes exactly in this direction.' Betroffensein is the pre-articulate condition of logos.

Gadamer p. 60: 'It is the same dynamis!' Rhetorical dynamis = hermeneutic capacity to understand. The closing extension (p. 62): 'rhetoric is, by far, not yet a possible word for what it itself is. In the end it is a communal listening.' Rhetoric/hermeneutics are coextensive in Gadamer's mature reading.
Gadamer p. 60: '[Sprachlichkeit means] everything that can allow something to be understood. Therefore, hermeneutics; thereby its indefinability.' Sprachlichkeit *is* hermeneutics in Gadamer's terms.

'In truth, rhetoric is the overarching concept for everything that has to do with the other' (p. 60). Rhetoric subsumes Sprachlichkeit at the volume's broad-rhetoric level (Kühne-Bertram & Rodi position).

Heidegger refused conversation: 'It was very difficult to speak with Heidegger because he wanted to understand step by step. So he did not terribly much like to discuss with me' (p. 50). Gadamer's hermeneutics privileges Gespräch *against* this Heideggerian refusal.
VT1 instantiation. Gadamer's rhetoric-as-dynamis-of-Mitsein (P1) supports the 'centrality' side; Pöggeler's restriction-thesis takes the opposite. The volume's frame keeps both visible.

Gadamer's pathē-as-fundamental-possibilities reading (P3) supports Gross's pathos-as-ontological-substrate thesis at the conceptual level; the bewährt caveat partially aligns with Hyde's argumentative-resource reading but the substrate-side is dominant.

GA 18, 117's pathē-as-fundamental-possibilities is operationalized in BT §29 as Befindlichkeit. Gadamer's terminology slides between the two without distinguishing them, treating the SS 1924 → BT bridge as transparent.
GA 18, 169f (n. 8): 'philosophers could decide to consider what speaking to others really means.' The locus directly defines/foregrounds the concept.

GA 63, 327 (n. 13): 'The actual being of a teacher is: to stand before an other and to speak to him, and in such a way that the other, listening, follows him.' Operationalizes speaking-to-others as the *being* of teaching.

'No one who expresses something says what he really means. Because no one can ever have the last word' (p. 60). Hermeneutics presupposes logos's structural incompleteness; without it, 'last-word' closure would replace conversation.

p. 61: 'Phronēsis is a whole virtue; it is not an ability, but a being.' The phronēsis-as-hexis claim parallels the rhetoric-as-dynamis claim and refines it: rhetoric and phronēsis are both *being-conditions*, not skills.

p. 61: 'A philosophical rhetoric would take the political into account, but not be absorbed into the political. ... Phronēsis is a whole virtue.' The rhetoric-politics balance depends structurally on phronēsis-as-virtue: only because phronēsis is not a technē can rhetoric-and-politics be bound without being identical.

p. 56: Heidegger's 'retreat out of politics' contributed to his 'neglect of nonpoetic forms of speaking ... poetic interpretation was his weakest area.' The political failure correlates structurally with the poetics-only turn, both as forms of withdrawal from rhetorical-political engagement.

Aristotle's Rhet. II catalog of pathē is operationalized in GA 18, 117 as 'the fundamental possibilities, by which Dasein primarily orients itself.' The translation Aristotle → Heidegger transforms the pathē-list from rhetorical-tactical to existential-fundamental.

p. 48: 'Plato's Symposium ... "You will not understand what I will now say." ... that's the origin of my hermeneutics.' Plato Symposium's last phase is the explicit origin of Gadamer's hermeneutic finitude doctrine.
p. 59 (n. 24): pathei mathos as 'the decisive statement' on linguisticality-attunement relation; learning through experience without epistemological intermediary. Aeschylus is the textual source.

Gadamer's defense at p. 55 affirms-and-limits Heidegger's political failure ('he erred when he did this' + 'sole university president ... did not retain his presidency for even one year'). The position partially undermines Heidegger's hermeneutic authority by acknowledging the political error, while limiting the cancellation move via factual proportion.

n. 17 = Die Sprache (1950) in Unterwegs zur Sprache, 32. Heidegger's 'living of mortals in the speaking of language' formula explains *Sprachlichkeit* in its later-Heideggerian register; Kemmann (p. 55) notes that Heidegger 'avoided returning again explicitly to rhetoric' in this register.

section_11_summary_one_paragraph: This interview, conducted across 1999-2001 with Hans-Georg Gadamer (interviewer Ansgar Kemmann; translator Lawrence Kennedy Schmidt), is the volume's primary first-person witness to Heidegger's pedagogical and philosophical practice in 1923-24. Gadamer testifies to the SS 1924 lecture course's *dynamis*-rather-than-*technē* definition of rhetoric (GA 18, 114) — quoted at the volume's locus classicus on tension VT2 — and traces this Aristotle reading forward to his own hermeneutics, which is at once an extension and a corrective: Gadamer privileges *Gespräch* over *Vortrag* and *Betroffensein* as the pre-articulate ground over Heidegger's pathē-doctrine. The four sections build cumulatively: (I) biographical foundations (1923 Freiburg, the 1923 phronēsis seminar, classical philology under Lommatzsch and Friedländer, Plato's Symposium as origin); (II) the *technē/dynamis* dispute as the volume's central rhetorical question; (III) Heidegger as rhetorically masterful but anti-conversational lecturer (Hartmann, Husserl, Bultmann, Scheler, Arendt as foils; the de partibus animae/animal anecdote as exemplum); (IV) the *Sprachlichkeit*-rhetoric-hermeneutics convergence on the formula 'It is the same dynamis!' (p. 60). Closing themes — *pathei mathos*, *bewährt* pathos, every logos is incomplete, communal listening, rhetoric's binding of politics without absorption — set up the volume's continuing engagement with VT2 (rhetoric as dynamis vs. technē), VT3 (continuity vs. rupture in Heidegger), VT5 (pathos as cognitive vs. ontological), and VT6 (hermeneutics displacing rhetoric). The 31 endnotes are extraordinarily citation-dense: 11 of 31 are GA 18 page references (notes 7, 10, 12, 16, 18, 19, 20, 22, 25, 27, 29 — the last drawn from Bröcker's transcript prior to GA 18's 2002 publication), with 3 GA 63 references (notes 10, 12, 13), the GA 26 Scheler obituary (n. 9), the *Natorp Report* (n. 1), and 'Die Sprache' 1950 (n. 17) — making the chapter the volume's primary cross-pipeline bridge to BCAP and a rich seed for cross-links to BT (Befindlichkeit, Schweigen) and to GA 63 / GA 26 / Unterwegs zur Sprache as currently un-indexed Heidegger pipeline candidates.
